title: Untitled (working title): the cold open
description: The cold open of an animated 1975 feature: a pilot who sounds amazed, a crate marked INERT, a truck, a near-miss, and a crate that is empty. About six minutes, 8 scenes, 39 shots, almost no dialogue, in the house style Painted Americana '75, with a painted board on every shot.

acts.title: Cold open: 1944 to the creek
acts.description: A pilot, a hangar, a truck, a swerve, a fall and an empty crate. Nobody says what it is.

scenes.title: Over Europe, 1944
scenes.description: The cockpit of a fighter over Europe, 1944, heard and never seen: engine drone, radio hiss and two voices. The screen stays black.
scenes.lightingNotes: No picture. Pure black while a radio talks; nothing is lit and nothing fades up.

scenes.title: Hangar 18
scenes.description: Hangar 18 at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, night, 1975: airmen quietly emptying the hangar under sodium lamps while a Senate hearing murmurs from a guard-booth television. One crate sits apart from the rest.
scenes.lightingNotes: Sodium-yellow work lamps under the hangar roof, wet concrete, the guard booth's blue television glow, one bare lamp over the lone crate; cold blue night at the open doors.

scenes.title: The back road
scenes.description: A truck and trailer on a twisting two-lane in the Ohio hills (leafy hardwood woods in summer), around 1 a.m.: fog in the hollows, warm dashboard light against the blue night, an unmarked sedan a quarter mile behind. An American left-hand-drive cab: a civilian trucker (driver's seat on the LEFT) and a young airman in civilian clothes (passenger, on the right) sit in it.
scenes.lightingNotes: Warm amber dashboard glow on faces, a green radio dial, deep blue night through the windshield; headlight cones lifting fog in the hollows; the sedan's headlights tiny and white far behind.

scenes.title: The swerve
scenes.description: A blind bend on the back road at night in leafy Ohio hardwood woods: the truck and trailer meeting a station wagon driven by a nurse coming off a double shift. Headlights, fog, a gravel shoulder and a drop to one side.
scenes.lightingNotes: Only the two vehicles' headlights sweeping the trunks, brake-light red flashes, dust and fog; no other light.

scenes.title: The fall
scenes.description: A wooded bank above a creek, night, Ohio hardwoods in full summer leaf: moonlit trunks and ferns, a loaded crate on its way down, and the dark inside the crate.
scenes.lightingNotes: Almost none: moonlight in slats between the trunks, flashes of pale sky through the crate's cracks; black tree verticals.

scenes.title: Topside
scenes.location: EXT. THE ROADSIDE, ABOVE THE BANK
scenes.description: The back road above the bank, night, just after the bend (leafy Ohio hardwoods, yellow centre line): road flares, red-lit fog, an unmarked sedan with two men in suits, a trucker and an airman. A white nurse's cap and a snapped-off side mirror lie on the asphalt.
scenes.lightingNotes: Red road flares are the only key light: hard crimson, sparks, red-lit fog; the sedan's white headlights as backlight; no flashlight beams.

scenes.title: The crate
scenes.description: The creek bank, night, Ohio hardwoods in leaf: a split-open crate in the shallows, a hollow in old packing straw, a board stenciled INERT, and flares held low.
scenes.lightingNotes: A hand-held flare, crimson, raking across scratched wood; the creek reflecting red; the far corner left in darkness.

scenes.title: Far off in the woods
scenes.location: EXT. THE WOODS ABOVE THE CREEK
scenes.description: The woods above the creek, night, moments later, Ohio hardwoods in leaf: the flare burning down, three men standing in silence, and the dark beyond the trees.
scenes.lightingNotes: The last dying orange of a flare against a moonlit tree line, then total black.

frames.title: Black: the radio
frames.description: Black screen. Radio hiss, the drone of an engine, and a pilot who sounds amazed, not scared: "It's copying me."
frames.lightingNotes: No light at all. A pure black frame; nothing fades up and nothing is hinted at.
frames.mood: Hushed and amazed, not afraid: a young man talking to himself over an engine.
frames.notes:
Sound: Engine drone, radio hiss, wind. Red Two close and breathy; Red Leader tinny and far. The clicks do not arrive until the next shot.
Framing: Hold black for the whole radio exchange. No title, no credit, no music.
RED TWO: (hushed) Red Leader, I've got something on my right wing.
RED LEADER: (clipped) Say again, Red Two.
RED TWO: (hushed) No markings. It's glowing. I bank, it banks. It's copying me.
Script: "BLACK SCREEN. Before any picture, a radio hiss and the drone of an engine."

Style: Painted Americana '75 (hand-drawn characters with weight over gouache backgrounds, dashboard amber against blue night). The painted board on this card was made against the continuity sheets in public/images/hangar/ (docs/hangar/README.md). The thing in the crate is never named, shown or described.

audio.text: Red Leader, I've got something on my right wing.
No markings. It's glowing. I bank, it banks. It's copying me.

frames.title: Three quick, one slow
frames.description: Still black. The clicking in the headset: three quick, one slow. This is the film's signature sound; record it once and use it everywhere.
frames.lightingNotes: Still pure black.
frames.notes:
Sound: The clicks arrive in his headset: three quick, one slow, close and dry, like a relay or a tongue on teeth. This exact recording is reused in the trailer and in the woods. Filter it slightly, as if heard through a headset.
Framing: Still black. The first thing we ever see is nothing.
RED LEADER: (clipped) Could be a Jerry trick. Take it down.
RED TWO: (hushed) It's not doing anything. It's just flying with me.
RED LEADER: (clipped) That's an order.
Script: "In his headset, a strange clicking, in a distinct rhythm: three quick, one slow."

audio.text: Could be a Jerry trick. Take it down.
It's not doing anything. It's just flying with me.

frames.title: Gunfire, then silence
frames.description: A long pause. Gunfire. Silence. We never see what he shot: hold the black.
frames.lightingNotes: Still pure black.
frames.mood: Dread: an order obeyed too late to be undone.
frames.notes:
Sound: Two short bursts, then true silence: drop the engine and the hiss out entirely for a full beat. The silence is the cut.
Framing: Hold black through the exchange, the pause and the gunfire. Do not cut to a picture of what he shot, ever.
Script: "A long pause. Then gunfire. Then silence."

frames.title: Wright-Patterson at night
frames.description: Fade up on the base: hangar doors open on yellow light, airmen moving crates in the dark, a truck backed to the door. Painted night, wet concrete, one flag.
frames.lightingNotes: Sodium-yellow work lamps strung under the hangar roof, wet concrete reflecting them, a cold blue night sky above the open doors, one lit window in the guard booth. No moon.
frames.mood: Hushed bustle: a secret being cleaned up quietly, in the dark.
frames.notes:
Sound: Idle generators, boots, a forklift's reversing beeper, insects. No score.
Framing: Open high over the apron and crane down to the hangar doors: the truck reversed up to the doors with its trailer's rear doors at the opening and the cab pointing away, soldiers small against enormous doors, a flag hanging limp, crates moving out in a slow line.
Script: "Fade up on Wright-Patterson at night."

frames.title: The guard-booth TV
frames.description: A small television in the guard booth: a Senate hearing, flickering. A voice: "what else has been kept from the American people." Nobody in the booth looks up.
frames.lightingNotes: The television's blue-white flicker is the only light inside the booth; the rest of the room is dim and warm brown.
frames.notes:
Sound: Muffled hearing audio from the booth's television, a gavel; the emptied hangar beyond.
Framing: Locked-off insert on a small curved-glass TV with rabbit ears: a committee table, a gavel. Nobody in the booth looks up.
TV: (muffled) ...the question before this committee is what else has been kept from the American people.
Script: "A TV in the guard booth shows a Senate hearing while airmen quietly empty the hangar."

audio.text: ...the question before this committee is what else has been kept from the American people.

frames.title: WRIGHT FIELD 1944 - INERT
frames.description: One crate sits apart from the rest, stenciled WRIGHT FIELD 1944 - INERT. Nobody reads it aloud.
frames.lightingNotes: One bare lamp directly over the crate: hard top light, deep shadow beneath it, the rest of the floor already empty and dark.
frames.mood: Ordinary and ominous: a label that has done its job for thirty years.
frames.notes:
Sound: The echo of an emptied hangar. The crate is silent.
Framing: Low angle from the floor so the crate looms. The stencil is weathered and legible. The coffee ring in the lid is visible but not yet explained. No push-in; nobody reads it aloud.
Script: "One crate sits apart from the others, stenciled WRIGHT FIELD 1944 - INERT. Nobody reads it aloud."

frames.title: The coffee ring
frames.description: The sergeant sets his cup on the lid, exactly into a ring worn into the wood. Then he remembers, and picks it back up.
frames.lightingNotes: Warm lamp light on the lid; steam from the cup backlit; the ring in the wood darker than the grain.
frames.mood: Habit, and a tenderness he would deny.
frames.notes:
Sound: Ceramic on wood, a small tick.
Framing: Top-down insert: the cup sits exactly in the ring worn into the lid. He lifts it away as the shot ends.
Script: "sets his coffee cup on the lid, right into a ring worn into the wood."

frames.title: Hand flat on the lid
frames.description: On his way past, the sergeant rests his hand flat on the lid, the way you would steady a sleeping animal.
frames.lightingNotes: Soft warm bounce from the work lamp on the weathered back of his hand; the lid itself cool and blue.
frames.mood: Quiet reverence: the way you steady a sleeping animal.
frames.notes:
Sound: A held breath. The hangar's emptiness. No knock yet: the crate stays silent here.
Framing: Hold on the hand and the lid. He does not look at the crate. Nothing answers.
Script: "he rests his hand flat on the lid, the way you would steady a sleeping animal."

frames.title: Don't you want to know?
frames.description: The airman holds out a clipboard. The trucker signs without looking up. AGRICULTURAL EQUIPMENT on the manifest.
frames.lightingNotes: Sodium lamp rim light on both men; the clipboard in a warm pool; the truck's red tail-lights behind them.
frames.notes:
Sound: A pen scratching the clipboard; the truck idling.
Framing: Two-shot at shoulder height. The trucker never looks up from signing; the airman's eyes go past him to the crate.
AIRMAN: Don't you want to know what's in it?
TRUCKER: (flat) Nope.
Script: "Don't you want to know what's in it?"

frames.title: Past the weigh station
frames.description: The truck blows past a sign ordering all trucks into the weigh station, and keeps going.
frames.lightingNotes: Headlights and the weigh station's amber floodlights sliding over the truck; deep blue night; the sign lit from below.
frames.mood: Defiance in motion: the paperwork skipped.
frames.notes:
Sound: Diesel, tyre hum, air brakes unused.
Framing: Wide tracking alongside as the truck passes the sign ordering all trucks into the weigh station, and keeps going.
Script: "The truck blows past a sign ordering all trucks into the weigh station."

frames.title: Into the hills
frames.description: A twisting two-lane climbing into the Ohio hills. Fog in the hollows, warm dash light against the blue night, an unmarked sedan a quarter mile back.
frames.lightingNotes: Deep blue twilight sky, fog in the hollows glowing faintly, the truck's headlights and, far behind, the sedan's, as two pinpricks.
frames.mood: Wonder and isolation: a big dark country and one small warm light.
frames.notes:
Sound: Crickets under the engine; wind swelling.
Framing: Crane up from the road to reveal the sweep of the hills in layered painted ridgelines of blue (Ghibli depth). The trailer is a small lit box on a very large night.
Script: "It turns onto a twisting two-lane and climbs into the Ohio hills"

frames.title: The cab
frames.description: Warm dash lights. The trucker grumbles: "First time anybody paid me to skip a scale." The airman in civilian clothes, hands on his knees.
frames.lightingNotes: Amber dashboard glow on both faces, a green radio dial, cool blue night through the windshield, the fog beyond.
frames.notes:
Sound: AM radio low under it (an old ballad), gearbox, tyres.
Framing: Medium two-shot from the dash. American left-hand-drive truck: the trucker sits on the truck's LEFT, so from the dash looking back at them he is on the viewer's RIGHT and the airman on the viewer's LEFT. The airman's clothes are civilian and too neat; the trucker wears a cap and his brown leather jacket; the wheel is large in frame.
TRUCKER: (dry) Thirty years driving. First time anybody paid me to skip a scale.
Script: "First time anybody paid me to skip a scale."

audio.text: Thirty years driving. First time anybody paid me to skip a scale.

frames.title: A knock from the trailer
frames.description: Then another. They both look back through the rear window at the dark trailer. "Load's shifting."
frames.lightingNotes: Dash glow on the backs of their heads; the red of the rear-view mirror; the black trailer visible through the sliding rear window.
frames.notes:
Sound: Knock. Knock: dull, wooden, inside the trailer.
Framing: Over the shoulder, looking back through the rear window at the dark trailer. The knock is heard before anyone looks.
TRUCKER: (flat) Load's shifting.
Script: "A knock from the trailer. Then another. They both look back."

frames.title: One-two-three... four
frames.description: The airman begins to tap his knee along with the knocks, under his breath: three quick, one slow.
frames.lightingNotes: Dash glow on his face and hand; the knee in the foreground in warm light.
frames.mood: Discovery: the first person to listen.
frames.notes:
Sound: Knocks and taps in unison: three quick, one slow.
Framing: Close on his hand tapping his knee. He is the passenger on the truck's right, so the wheel is on his LEFT — it sits across the cab at the left of frame, never under his hand. The taps lock to the knocks coming off-screen.
AIRMAN: (murmured) One-two-three... four. One-two-three... four.
Script: "One-two-three... four. One-two-three... four."

Style: Painted Americana '75 (hand-drawn characters with weight over gouache backgrounds, dashboard amber against blue night). The painted board on this card was made against the continuity sheets in public/images/hangar/ (docs/hangar/README.md). The thing in the crate is never named, shown or described.
Retake (7 October 2026): the corrected take is installed; the outgoing study is archived at public/images/hangar/archive/s3/14-one-two-three-four--v1.jpg. The wheel reads across the cab at the left of frame, unmistakably the driver's; the tapping hand is the young passenger's.

frames.title: The slow one never arrives
frames.description: Three quick knocks. No fourth. He waits, one finger raised, in silence. "There. Settled."
frames.lightingNotes: Faces nearly in silhouette against headlight glare; the dash glow dims.
frames.notes:
Sound: Three quick knocks. Silence where the fourth should be: take the engine down for half a second.
Framing: Extreme close-up of his raised finger, then his eyes. Hold longer than is comfortable.
TRUCKER: (flat) There. Settled.
Script: "Three quick knocks. The slow one never arrives."

frames.title: Headlights round the bend
frames.description: A station wagon comes around the bend, drifting over the center line.
frames.lightingNotes: Wagon headlights sweep across the trunks and flare into the lens; the road goes white; fog.
frames.notes:
Sound: Gravel under a tyre; a ballad on the wagon's radio, faint.
Framing: Locked wide at the bend, the yellow centre line running through the shot. The wagon drifts over it a beat too long; Ohio hardwoods in full summer leaf crowd both sides — no redwood trunks, no bare winter branches.
Script: "A station wagon comes around the bend, drifting over the center line."

frames.title: Two more miles
frames.description: The nurse, window down to stay awake, eyes heavy: "Come on. Two more miles."
frames.lightingNotes: Dash glow on her face and white cap; cold night air from the open window; oncoming headlights cross her eyes at the end of the shot.
frames.notes:
Sound: Night air through the open window, her own breath, the wagon's radio ballad.
Framing: Close on her eyes. The window beside her is fully down — no glass in the frame — and the night air is lifting her hair. A slow blink; the lids drop. She wears the same white cap with its one thin red band as the sheet, and a hospital ID clipped to her coat, blurred but readable as a badge (the evidence seed).
MOM: (drowsy) Come on. Two more miles.
Script: "Come on. Two more miles."

frames.title: Both drivers yank the wheel
frames.description: Horn and tires. The wagon scrapes past the truck's cab with inches to spare.
frames.lightingNotes: Headlights strobing across the windscreens; brake-lights flaring red.
frames.notes:
Sound: Horn, tyre shriek, gravel.
Framing: Handheld, low. Truck and wagon pass head-on in opposite directions, one showing its front and the other its tail, the wagon drifting into the truck's lane; the nurse is alone in the wagon. The wagon's flank slides past the truck's cab by a hand's width. Draw the motion with smears, not blur; keep the weight of both vehicles.
Script: "Both drivers yank the wheel."

frames.title: The mirror, the cap
frames.description: Her side mirror snaps off. Her nurse's cap flies out of the window and spins down onto the asphalt.
frames.lightingNotes: Red tail-light wash on the road; the cap lit white by a headlight sweep; the mirror's glass catches it.
frames.notes:
Sound: Snap of metal, a glass skitter, the cap's soft slap.
Framing: Insert, low: the mirror snaps off and skitters; the cap spins down onto the asphalt. Keep both clearly in frame so the audience remembers them.
Script: "its side mirror snaps off and her nurse's cap flies out of the window."

frames.title: The skid
frames.description: The trailer fishtails across the road, headlights swinging across the trees.
frames.lightingNotes: Headlights swinging across tree trunks in long ribbons; dust; brake-lights.
frames.mood: The weight of a truck losing the road.
frames.notes:
Sound: Tyre howl, chains rattling.
Framing: Tracking wide beside the trailer as it fishtails; follow the rear doors.
Script: "The trailer fishtails"

frames.title: The missing knock
frames.description: In the middle of the skid, the slow knock lands, hard. The rear doors burst open. We cannot tell whether the skid threw them or something inside did.
frames.lightingNotes: The rear doors lit only by the truck's tail-lights; the interior behind them pure black.
frames.notes:
Sound: The missing fourth knock, huge and near; the metal bang of the doors bursting.
Framing: Medium at the trailer's rear doors. The slow knock lands from inside at the same instant the skid peaks; the latch lets go. Never show the inside. Neither a push nor a bump: it must read both ways.
Script: "the missing slow knock lands, hard."

frames.title: Over the edge
frames.description: The crate slides out of the trailer and over the edge of the bank.
frames.lightingNotes: Tail-lights follow the crate to the lip of the bank, then black.
frames.notes:
Sound: Wood scraping on metal, then the first crack of impact far below.
Framing: Locked wide. The crate slides; one beat of nothing; it tips and is gone.
Script: "The crate slides out and over the edge."

frames.title: Down the bank
frames.description: The crate tumbles through the trees, shedding boards, slamming into trunks.
frames.lightingNotes: Moonlight in slats between the trunks; no key light; boards flash pale blue as they fly off.
frames.notes:
Sound: Impacts: each tree a different thud, then splintering. No clicks.
Framing: Wide tracking down with the crate. The trees are hard dark verticals; boards peel away.
Script: "The crate tumbles down the wooded bank, slamming into trees and shedding boards."

frames.title: Inside the crate
frames.description: The camera rides inside with it: darkness, flashes of light through the cracks, nothing you can make out.
frames.lightingNotes: Black, with stuttering slivers of moonlight through the cracks; no fill.
frames.notes:
Sound: Muffled thumps; a rattle like breath. No click.
Framing: POV from inside, handheld, thrown with the crate. Nothing recognizable. Never reveal what is in there.
Script: "The camera rides inside with it: darkness, flashes of light through the cracks, nothing you can make out."

frames.title: By the creek
frames.description: It lands by the creek, split open. Silence. Then the crickets start up again.
frames.lightingNotes: Pale blue moonlight on the split boards; a glint on the creek; straw spilling out.
frames.notes:
Sound: Silence, then crickets fading up, then the creek.
Framing: Wide, locked off. Moonlight only: no moon disc in frame, no red light on the crate and nothing red in the water that could read as blood. The crate is the prop sheet's — steel straps, stenciled boards, no hinged fittings. Hold for five full seconds before the crickets begin.
Script: "It lands by the creek, split open."

Style: Painted Americana '75 (hand-drawn characters with weight over gouache backgrounds, dashboard amber against blue night). The painted board on this card was made against the continuity sheets in public/images/hangar/ (docs/hangar/README.md). The thing in the crate is never named, shown or described.
Retake (7 October 2026): the corrected take is installed; the outgoing study is archived at public/images/hangar/archive/s5/25-by-the-creek--v1.jpg. Nothing red in or on the water and nothing but straw in the crate. Caveat, honestly: the moonlit blue reads brighter than this scene's almost-none note — the content is right and the key is the director's call.

frames.title: Taillights
frames.description: The wagon's taillights disappear around the bend. She didn't stop.
frames.lightingNotes: Two red taillights shrinking round the bend; blue-black trees.
frames.notes:
Sound: Her engine fading, the ballad on her radio carrying on a moment longer.
Framing: Locked wide. The wagon does not brake, and its two red tail-lights are two distinct points, the only bright thing in the frame, with the yellow centre line running away to it. The road empties.

characters.name: Red Two
characters.description: A fighter pilot over Europe, heard and never seen. He sounds amazed, not scared. He does not want to fire.

characters.name: Red Leader
characters.description: Gives the order. Assumes a trick from the Germans ("a Jerry trick").

characters.name: Airman
characters.description: Sent along in civilian clothes to see the load safely off the base. He is the first to notice the knocks are a rhythm, and the only one who hears the clicks at the end.

characters.name: Sergeant
characters.description: Has watched these crates for decades. Sets his coffee on the lid out of habit, then rests his hand flat on it, the way you would steady a sleeping animal. Did he know it was awake?

characters.name: Trucker
characters.description: Thirty years on the road. Signs for AGRICULTURAL EQUIPMENT without looking up. The only joke in the open is his.

characters.name: Mom
characters.description: Coming off a double shift, window down to stay awake, nodding off at the wheel. Never stops. Never knows what she nearly hit, or what she left behind: her side mirror and her cap.

characters.name: Agent
characters.description: Arrive in an unmarked sedan. One pockets the nurse's cap and the snapped-off mirror: the thread to the boy's house.

notes.title: Start here: what this is
notes.content: Working title only. This is the cold open of an animated 1970s feature about a boy, a small machine nobody can name, and the people hunting for it. It runs about six minutes: a pilot's voice in 1944, a hangar emptied in 1975, a truck on a back road, a near-miss, a crate that falls, and a crate that is empty. The Screenplay tab holds the pages; the Storyboard has 39 painted boards drawn against the continuity sheets in public/images/hangar/. Acts one to three come next.

notes.title: The look: Painted Americana '75
notes.content:
Painted, not photographed: warm dashboard amber against deep blue night, gouache fog in the hollows, soft hand-painted skies. Characters are drawn plainly and with weight, with strong silhouettes and believable acting, in the manner of 1950s to 1970s American animation (wood paneling, station wagons, diner chrome, AM radios).

The Iron Giant for the people, Studio Ghibli for the places. People and vehicles have real mass: no squash and stretch, no cartoon takes; motion is drawn with smears, not blur. Backgrounds are layered multiplane paintings with atmosphere in every layer: fog, cloud, wet leaves, weathered paint. Light always comes from something in the world: dashboard amber, hangar sodium, road-flare crimson, moon blue. Gentle film grain, soft halation on lamps, 16:9 full-bleed. The camera is patient and leaves room for silence. It is the house style 'Painted Americana '75' in every shot's style picker, and every scene and shot in this workspace already carries it.

notes.title: Seeds the cold open plants
notes.content:
1. The nurse's cap and the snapped-off mirror lead the agents and the detective to the boy's house by different routes.
2. The rhythm (three quick, one slow) ties the airman, the pilot and the machine together before any character notices.
3. The uncrossed marks in the dark corner are the act-two flip: it was not counting days served, it was counting days left. Decide the exact number now; it sets the length of the film's clock.
4. The coffee ring leaves an open question: did the sergeant know it was awake?
5. The airman is the only one who hears the clicks at the end: he is the government's way in to the boy, and the audience's.

notes.title: Rules and sound
notes.content: Nobody says alien, robot or UFO. Flares, not flashlight beams, outdoors. One recording of the three-quick-one-slow rhythm, used in 1944, in the trailer and in the woods. Never show what the pilot shot; never show what is in the crate. The 1975 setting is deliberate: Church Committee, post-Watergate paranoia, Blue Book already closed.

notes.title: Open questions
notes.content: Title. Why does it move now, after thirty years? How many uncrossed marks (the film's clock)? Is the sergeant the old pilot? Does the airman cross sides? What is the exact count of marks the agents see? The robot's origin stays unexplained: a 1944 shoot-down, bodies and one small machine sent to Wright-Patterson.

brainstorm.title: The boy
brainstorm.content: 11. His mum works double shifts; he is alone at night and rides his bike in the woods. Both of them are waiting for someone who is not coming back. His dad left.

brainstorm.title: The machine
brainstorm.content: Rounded, worn, nothing like a lab. It does not say what it is. It copies sounds. The clicking is its first word.

brainstorm.title: The detective
brainstorm.content: An ex-debunker from Project Blue Book (Wright-Patterson was its headquarters). Spent a career explaining things away; now has to listen to the people he used to dismiss.

brainstorm.title: The battery
brainstorm.content: It has been running on almost nothing for thirty years, playing dead. Being awake with the boy spends what it saved. The marks are the clock.

brainstorm.title: The government
brainstorm.content: Do not know what they have. The scarier for it. They are about to make the same mistake as 1944: shoot first.

script:
Title: Untitled (working title)
Credit: The cold open
Author: [Your Name]
Draft date: October 2026

===

>THE LOOK<

Ohio, 1975, painted rather than photographed: warm dashboard light against blue night, fog in the hollows, wood paneling and station wagons. Soft hand-painted backgrounds and weather; characters drawn plainly and with weight. Small-town Americana that makes something strange feel real.

Nobody in this film ever says "alien", "robot" or "UFO".

>THE SOUND<

Three quick clicks, one slow. It is the same recording over a pilot's headset in 1944, as knocks inside a trailer in 1975, and far off in the woods at the end.

===

INT. COCKPIT, OVER EUROPE - 1944 #1#

BLACK SCREEN. Before any picture, a radio hiss and the drone of an engine.

RED TWO (V.O.)
Red Leader, I've got something on my right wing.

RED LEADER (V.O.)
Say again, Red Two.

RED TWO (V.O.)
No markings. It's glowing. I bank, it banks. It's copying me.

In his headset, a strange clicking, in a distinct rhythm: three quick, one slow.

RED LEADER (V.O.)
Could be a Jerry trick. Take it down.

RED TWO (V.O.)
It's not doing anything. It's just flying with me.

RED LEADER (V.O.)
That's an order.

A long pause. Then gunfire. Then silence. We never see what he shot.

INT. HANGAR 18, WRIGHT-PATTERSON - NIGHT, 1975 #2#

Fade up on Wright-Patterson at night. A TV in the guard booth shows a Senate hearing while airmen quietly empty the hangar.

TV (V.O.)
...the question before this committee is what else has been kept from the American people.

One crate sits apart from the others, stenciled WRIGHT FIELD 1944 - INERT. Nobody reads it aloud.

An old SERGEANT, who has watched these crates for decades, sets his coffee cup on the lid, right into a ring worn into the wood. Then he remembers, and picks it back up. On his way past, he rests his hand flat on the lid, the way you would steady a sleeping animal.

A young AIRMAN hands a clipboard to a civilian TRUCKER.

AIRMAN
Don't you want to know what's in it?

TRUCKER
(signing without looking up)
Nope.

The manifest reads AGRICULTURAL EQUIPMENT.

EXT./INT. TRUCK, BACK ROAD - NIGHT #3#

The truck blows past a sign ordering all trucks into the weigh station. It turns onto a twisting two-lane and climbs into the Ohio hills: fog in the hollows, warm dash lights against the blue night. The Airman rides along in civilian clothes. An unmarked sedan trails a quarter mile back.

TRUCKER
Thirty years driving. First time anybody paid me to skip a scale.

A knock from the trailer. Then another. They both look back.

TRUCKER (CONT'D)
Load's shifting.

The Airman starts tapping his knee along with it, under his breath.

AIRMAN
One-two-three... four. One-two-three... four.

Three quick knocks. The slow one never arrives. He waits, one finger raised, in silence.

TRUCKER
There. Settled.

EXT. THE BEND, BACK ROAD - NIGHT #4#

A station wagon comes around the bend, drifting over the center line. The driver is a NURSE coming off a double shift, window down to stay awake, nodding off. She is the boy's MOM.

MOM
(to herself)
Come on. Two more miles.

Both drivers yank the wheel. The wagon scrapes past; its side mirror snaps off and her nurse's cap flies out of the window. The trailer fishtails, and in the middle of the skid the missing slow knock lands, hard. The rear doors burst open. We cannot tell whether the skid threw them or something inside did.

The crate slides out and over the edge.

EXT. WOODED BANK - NIGHT #5#

The crate tumbles down the wooded bank, slamming into trees and shedding boards. The camera rides inside with it: darkness, flashes of light through the cracks, nothing you can make out.

It lands by the creek, split open. Silence. Then the crickets start up again.

EXT. THE ROADSIDE, ABOVE THE BANK - NIGHT #6#

The wagon's taillights disappear around the bend. She didn't stop.

The Trucker lights road flares. The sedan screeches up and two men in suits get out. One of them, an AGENT, picks up the nurse's cap, white on the black asphalt in the red light, and the snapped-off mirror beside it. He pockets both.

AGENT
Where is it?

TRUCKER
(pointing down the bank, shaking)
Down there. Some lady in a wagon, she just came right at me.

The Agent looks at the white cap in his hand. Then the two agents and the Airman start down the bank through red fog.

EXT. THE CREEK BANK - NIGHT #7#

The crate is empty. A small hollow is pressed into thirty-year-old packing straw, where something lay curled up. A broken board stenciled INERT lies half-sunk in the creek.

An agent holds his flare low to the inside wall, and the light rakes across rows of tiny scratched marks, thousands of them, covering every inch. Each mark has a short stroke cut through it. The newest stroke is bright, fresh-cut wood.

It was counting.

The flare does not reach the far corner, where a few marks are still uncrossed. Nobody looks there.

EXT. THE WOODS ABOVE THE CREEK - NIGHT #8#

Far off in the woods, faintly: three quick clicks and one slow, moving away. The agents don't notice. The Airman does.

AIRMAN
(barely audible, lips moving)
One-two-three... four.

The flare sputters out.

CUT TO BLACK.

TITLE CARD.
